lenses.name: Adverse conduct next door
lenses.description: The join this whole realm was built to make. Take the money, resolve it to registered addresses, find who else is registered there, then ask the adverse registers about EVERY neighbour — not just the one that got paid. A funded provider whose co-tenants carry compliance actions is invisible in every published list, because no list crosses premises with conduct. Co-location is lawful and ordinary and a neighbour's record is not the funded entity's record: this produces an address, the entities at it, and each one's register position, for a human to read. It asserts no relationship between neighbours beyond a shared registered address.

lenses.name: Ask in plain English
lenses.description: Type a question and the platform generates the Cypher, runs it against the live registers, and shows BOTH the answer and the query it wrote. The generated query is the point: it is inspectable, re-runnable, and provably the thing that produced the rows — not a paraphrase of them.

params.name: question
params.label: Your question
params.default: which agencies signed the largest contracts last week?

lenses.name: Ask indexed parliamentary records
lenses.description: Answer an open-ended question from parliamentary records that the user previously indexed from ParlInfo. A bounded agentic-RAG loop reformulates and judges retrieval against the question, then a second grounded pass writes an answer using only the returned verbatim evidence. Every answer retains numbered evidence and the source record identity. This lens cannot search records that have not been indexed.

lenses.name: Awards clustered under thresholds
lenses.description: A pattern detector, fenced as one: agency–supplier pairs with several awards in the window each sitting just under a procurement threshold, summing over it. Splitting a requirement to avoid a threshold is prohibited by the Commonwealth Procurement Rules — but clustered small awards are ALSO what routine, legitimate ordering looks like. This lens finds the SHAPE and hands it to a human; it never claims intent, and no output of it may be read as a finding.

params.name: threshold
params.label: Threshold (AUD) — default $80k, the open-tender threshold for non-construction

lenses.name: Banned people who registered a business afterwards
lenses.description: A banning order stops a person providing NDIS supports. It does not stop them registering a business. This lens takes the individuals the NDIS Commission has banned, looks each family name up in the Australian Business Register — the only open source that dates registration for every Australian entity — and keeps the records where the GIVEN names also agree and the ABN's current status took effect AFTER the ban. The result is a list of PEOPLE TO CHECK, never people identified: names repeat, and an active ABN is not NDIS work — a banned support worker may lawfully run a cafe. What makes a row worth a human's time is the combination the lens prints in full: the ban's own words and dates, the new registration's date and trading names, and how close the two sit in time.

params.name: maxSubjects
params.label: Banned individuals to check (each is a full-register scan; keep small)

params.name: sinceDate
params.label: Only bans effective on or after

params.name: seasonDays
params.label: Only bans at least this many days old (a fresh ban cannot yet show a new registration)

params.name: assess
params.label: Read the ban narratives for what the person was doing (yes/no)

lenses.name: Contracts already near their end date
lenses.description: Of the contracts published in a window, which are already within a horizon of their stated end date — the renewal and re-tender pipeline, from the register's own period fields. States its own boundary plainly: this is what was PUBLISHED in the window and ends soon, not every Commonwealth contract ending soon, because the feed can only be read by id or publication date.

params.name: withinDays
params.label: Ending within this many days of today

lenses.name: Contracts that grew through amendments
lenses.description: The contracts whose value was amended UPWARD in a period, ranked by growth over the original commitment — the register's own before/after, computed from each notice's version chain. Two hops over the live feed: the change window finds WHICH contracts amended, then each notice's full chain gives original vs current. AusTender records commitments, so this measures a contract growing past what was first agreed — which is not a budget, and is never presented as one.

lenses.name: Contracts that never re-tender
lenses.description: Procurement that has quietly become permanent: contracts amended repeatedly in the change window, with their END DATES moving outward — serial extension instead of re-tender. Distinct from expiry tracking (au-short-dated finds honest endings); this finds the ones that never end. An extension can be entirely proper — this lens counts and dates, and hands a human the list.

lenses.name: Contracts vs tax paid
lenses.description: The window's winners against the ATO corporate tax transparency report: which suppliers taking large Commonwealth commitments reported nil-or-below-zero tax payable. Built-in caveats carried verbatim, because this join is easy to over-read: a BLANK tax payable means ≤ $0 BY LEGISLATION (never 'unknown'); the report is entity-level, not consolidated groups; and 2023-24 tax against this window's contracts is a timing mismatch. A flow worth knowing about — never an allegation.

lenses.name: Daily Briefing
lenses.description: Your morning brief — what's salient since a chosen point in time.

lenses.name: Deep dive on one contract
lenses.description: Everything the registers and the open web hold about one contract notice, in three clearly separated tiers: the REGISTER (what was signed, amended and stated), the CROSS-REGISTER context (the agency's portfolio, the ground's own text, the supplier's lobbying disclosures), and UNVERIFIED press coverage matched on a search phrase. The tiers never blend — coverage is material about the parties, never evidence about the contract.

params.name: searchPhrase
params.label: Coverage search phrase (blank = composed from supplier + agency)

lenses.name: Grants by electorate margin
lenses.description: Where discretionary money LANDS, politically: date-scoped grant awards mapped by their DELIVERY postcode (the only honest geographic basis — recipient addresses are head offices) onto the seeded electorates with their 2025 margins. Grants per dollar into marginal government-held seats vs safe seats. Election facts joined to published awards: it answers WHERE, and establishes nothing about WHY — every surface says so.

lenses.name: Grants that don't say what they fund
lenses.description: The grants analogue of thin contract disclosure, with a signal contracts don't have: the SAME purpose text published verbatim across many awards. A program that pastes one paragraph onto every grant has disclosed the PROGRAM, never the award — the reader cannot tell what any individual dollar bought. Three deterministic screens (missing, template-shared, or merely an echo of the activity or program name), then an LLM reading of what survives. A finding about the DISCLOSURE, never about the grant: a small community grant reasonably says less than a research council award, and the output is a prompt to go read the record.

lenses.name: How contracts avoided open tender
lenses.description: Which reason codes agencies used to go to limited tender or claim an exemption in a window, what they cost, and which agencies used them — with the register's OWN verbatim text for each code. Pure arithmetic over published fields; a stated ground is a recorded reason, never an assessment of one.

lenses.name: How to fix this failure
lenses.description: For one failed workflow run: the error lines from the failed job's log, what the web says about that error, and a resolution hint grounded on both with sources. "How do I fix run 123", "why did run 123 fail and what should I do", "resolution for this failure".

params.name: jobId
params.label: Job id (optional — the first failed job otherwise)

lenses.name: Index matching parliamentary records
lenses.description: Opt in to fetching and indexing a small, balanced set of ParlInfo records matching a phrase: up to two Chamber Hansard, two committee and two Senate Estimates records. The records are written to the user's document knowledge base under stable parlinfo:// identities so they can subsequently be searched semantically, including with the au-hansard-rag agentic lens.

params.name: phrase
params.label: Phrase whose matching records should be indexed

lenses.name: Integrity screen
lenses.description: The check no Commonwealth entity can run today: a window's contract winners (or one supplier) against the adverse and disclosure registers — NDIS compliance actions WITH temporal overlap against contract dates, Modern Slavery lodgement, and the ATO tax transparency report. No federal debarment register exists (CPR 6.9 substitutes tenderer self-declaration); these are the closest published substitutes, and every hit is a REGISTER ENTRY to hand a human, never a finding about a contract or a determination about an entity.

params.name: supplier
params.label: Or one supplier name (blank = screen the window's winners)

lenses.name: Is this supplier a registered lobbying client
lenses.description: Whether a name appears as a CLIENT on the federal Register of Lobbyists, which lobbying firms list it, and the register's own former-government-representative declarations for those firms' people. The register carries no client ABNs, so the supplier↔client join is a NAME match and is reported as one, with the matched strings shown. Facts from the register, verbatim — a lobbying relationship is a disclosure, never a finding.

params.name: supplierName
params.label: Supplier / company name as it appears on contracts

lenses.name: Money running while an action was in force
lenses.description: The temporal question the registers can't ask each other: whose Commonwealth money was RUNNING during the period an NDIS compliance action was in force against them — grants and contracts together, each matched by ABN and compared date-against-date. Overlap is the sharpest honest claim available from published data, and it is still only a claim about DATES. An action concerns a provider's NDIS obligations; money running at the same time may fund something else entirely, under a different program, in a different state. Actions are ranked by the register's own severity wording, because a banning order and a compliance notice are not the same object.

lenses.name: One ABN, every register
lenses.description: Everything the Commonwealth publishes about one ABN, in one place: contracts won, grants received, NDIS compliance actions, Modern Slavery lodgement, and the ATO tax transparency row. Each register is asked separately so a SILENCE is qualified per register — "not in this register", never "clean" — and no federal debarment register exists to ask. Grants and contracts are window scans narrowed by ABN, so their answer is bounded by the window, which the output states. Register entries to hand a human, never a determination about the entity.

lenses.name: One agency's procurement
lenses.description: Everything the register holds about how one agency bought in a period — total committed, the method split, its largest contracts, who it bought from, what it bought (the government's own category titles), and the grounds it stated when it did not go to open tender. The agency also resolves against the seeded AGOR spine for its portfolio, ABN and staffing, which the contract feed never carries.

lenses.name: One supplier's Commonwealth business
lenses.description: What one supplier won in a period — total committed, which agencies bought from them, how those contracts were procured (and the grounds stated when they were not open), what they supplied by the government's own category titles, and whether the federal lobbyist register lists them as a client. The register has no supplier search, so this fetches a window and narrows by name, which the answer states.

lenses.name: Providers sharing an address
lenses.description: The co-location join nobody can run today: which recipients of Commonwealth money are registered at the SAME street address as other charities. ASIC's company dataset carries no address, so this is only possible for the charity sector — but that is where much of the disability and community-services estate sits. Shared premises are routine and lawful: serviced offices, community hubs, auspicing arrangements, and a school's P&C at the school. A cluster is therefore a PLACE TO LOOK, never a finding, and no officer link is implied — no open Australian source publishes responsible-person names in bulk, so this lens cannot and does not claim one.

lenses.name: Said in Estimates vs signed in contracts
lenses.description: Rhetoric against procurement, both labelled: what a portfolio's officials said in INDEXED Estimates transcripts (semantic search over hearings you have indexed via au-parliament), beside what its agencies' contracts actually bought in the window. Two summaries, two sources, rendered side by side and never blended — each is a model's reduction of quoted material, and the lens says which material. Requires indexed hearings; without them it says so and stops.

lenses.name: Search what the Commonwealth signed
lenses.description: Search contract descriptions in a publication window, two ways it always discloses: KEYWORD is a deterministic case-insensitive containment match; SEMANTIC uses the engine's ai_relevant / ai_score primitives to keep and rank rows by fit to a natural-language ask ("anything about cyber security uplift"), and says a model judged the fit. Every hit carries its description, value, parties and a link to the AusTender record.

lenses.name: Shapes the regulator has not acted on
lenses.description: The compliance register lists providers already caught. This lens looks for the SHAPES that caught cases had — in the filings of providers with no register entry at all. Seven arithmetic screens over two years of the providers' own Annual Information Statements: a service-revenue surge with no matching staff growth; a filing that contradicts itself (government revenue above total revenue, staff expenses without staff); labour costs too thin for a workforce business at that scale; a workforce model that flipped from wages to something else in one year; money leaving as unspecified 'other expenses'; a first-ever filing already at multi-million scale; and a disability program declared last year and not this year. Each survivor is then checked against the NDIS compliance register — those with NO entry are the point of the lens — and only that shortlist is read subjectively: published coverage is fetched per name and per registered trading name, every item must LITERALLY NAME the organisation to be considered, and only those items are reduced to what they say, whether they report an allegation or action, and whether they explain a disappearance benignly. Generic sector coverage is discarded rather than judged, because a model asked "is this about X" will pass an article about the scheme as an article about X. Every row carries a stable findingKey so a scheduled run can report only what is NEW. A screen hit is an ANOMALY IN A SELF-REPORT, not an allegation: reporting-period changes, group restructures, capital grants and plain data-entry error produce every one of these shapes innocently, which is exactly why each row is a place to look and never a finding.

params.name: assess
params.label: Read published coverage for the shortlist (yes/no)

params.name: maxAssessed
params.label: Cap on entities sent for coverage reading

lenses.name: The accountability gap
lenses.description: Does scrutiny follow money? The window's largest commitments, each checked against the parliamentary record — Hansard debates, committee evidence and Estimates, searched by contract notice id through ParlInfo's own feeds. The coverage rate nobody publishes: how much of the period's money was EVER raised, and how much never appears. Silence is qualified (these record classes, this id as the phrase) — Questions on Notice are not yet searchable, so 'never raised in Parliament' stays off the table; 'not found in these records' is the honest maximum.

params.name: topN
params.label: How many of the largest contracts to check (each is one ParlInfo search)

lenses.name: The June rush
lenses.description: Use-it-or-lose-it, quantified: June's committed value per agency against that agency's own May baseline, from complete day-partitioned windows of the same register. A June multiple is a fact about TIMING of commitments — end-of-year contracting has legitimate drivers (annual renewals, budget certainty) — so this lens measures the spike and never diagnoses it.

lenses.name: The life of one Commonwealth contract
lenses.description: Every published version of one AusTender contract notice — the value curve through its amendments, who signed it, how it was procured (with the stated reason wherever the method was limited tender), and anything the description text records that the structured fields never carried. Every figure is the register's own; no model produces any number here.

lenses.name: The parliamentary record
lenses.description: Search Hansard directly for ANY topic — a policy area, a program, a supplier, an agency, a contract id: chamber debates, committee evidence and Senate Estimates transcripts matching the phrase, from ParlInfo's own records — grouped by record class, each hit linking to the transcript with its date, plus a date-scoped Estimates check over the chosen window. A match is a page where the phrase appears, never a finding about anyone; a silence is qualified per record class, and Questions on Notice are not yet searchable, so "never raised in Parliament" is a conclusion this lens refuses to support.

params.name: phrase
params.label: Search phrase — any topic (a policy area, a program, a supplier, an agency, a contract id)

params.name: from
params.label: Estimates window from (for the date-scoped check)

params.name: index
params.label: Index the followed transcripts into your documents (semantic search over them afterwards)

lenses.name: The provider ledger, reconstructed from the providers' own filings
lenses.description: The NDIA publishes no per-provider payments, so this lens reconstructs the ledger from the counterparties' own disclosures (docs/adr/0001): every ACNC-registered charity classified as serving people with disabilities, joined by ABN to its own FY2024 Annual Information Statement — self-reported government revenue, goods-and-services revenue (where NDIS fee-for-service often books), staff FTE, employee expenses, grants it made — then to the published Commonwealth money registers and the NDIS compliance register. Two arithmetic surfaces come out: the RESIDUAL (self-reported government revenue minus what GrantConnect and AusTender account for — the part of the public ledger no register itemizes), and the LOW-STAFF-HIGH-REVENUE shape (revenue a filing says was earned with almost no staff, almost no employee expense and almost no pass-through grants — the arithmetic a phantom-services claim would have to survive). Both are places to look, never findings; every number is the charity's own or the register's own.

params.name: scope
params.label: Candidates: 'programs' (self-classified disability programs) or 'roll' (whole beneficiary-flag roll)

lenses.name: The same work, funded from two places
lenses.description: Awards whose PURPOSES read as the same work, funded through different programs — or by different agencies entirely. Nobody can see this today: each program publishes its own list, and no view crosses them. Deterministic first (shared distinctive wording between two purposes, counted, with both texts shown), then an optional LLM read of the top pairs for whether they really describe the same work. Overlap is NOT duplication: co-funding is normal, staged programs are deliberate, and two grants can share language while funding different things. This produces PAIRS TO READ.

lenses.name: What a portfolio is actually buying
lenses.description: The subjective layer over the register's own prose. Contract CATEGORIES are UNSPSC codes ('50000000') and titles are internal references — neither tells you what a portfolio actually bought. The descriptions do, and this reduces them per portfolio with the engine's LLM aggregations: recurring themes, emergent clusters, a plain-language digest, and the single vaguest description for its value. Every number beside them stays arithmetic, and every model-produced field is labelled as a judgment.

params.name: portfolio
params.label: Portfolio (blank = every portfolio in the window)

lenses.name: What entered and left the compliance register
lenses.description: The register as a time series. The NDIS Commission publishes compliance actions as dated catalogue extracts, each CURRENT STATE only — so nothing published shows when an action appeared, and nothing at all shows when one disappeared. This lens enumerates every extract via the data.gov.au catalogue, diffs consecutive extracts, and reports both directions: an APPEARANCE is an enforcement event dated to a snapshot interval even where the register's own date is blank; a DISAPPEARANCE is classified against the row's own published end date — removal after expiry is lifecycle, removal while nominally in force is the signal nobody tracks. A removal is a fact about the register's contents and nothing more: the register does not say why a row left, and an ART overturn, a Commission correction, and a data error all look identical here.

params.name: followUp
params.label: Chase each durable removal into AustLII and the news index (yes/no)

lenses.name: What the Commonwealth signed in a period
lenses.description: Contract notices first published in a date window — total committed value, the procurement- method split (with every limited tender's stated reason available), and the largest contracts, suppliers and agencies. Pure arithmetic over the register's rows; a capped fetch is reported as PARTIAL, never passed off as the whole period.

lenses.name: What the regulator has told Parliament
lenses.description: Senate Estimates is where officials answer for the scheme on the record, and ParlInfo publishes the transcripts. This lens searches the Estimates record for the integrity vocabulary — banning orders, unregistered providers, fraud, compliance action — keeps only pages whose own excerpt contains that language, and reads what was said: a summary of the exchange, whether an official described providers RETURNING after enforcement, and whether the page names any provider. The excerpts are verbatim with ParlInfo's speaker attribution intact, because the value here is the quotation, not the paraphrase. A page is a page of the record: officials speak to policy and to patterns, and Estimates witnesses are frequently constrained from discussing an individual provider at all — so an absence of names is the venue's rule, never evidence that none exist.

params.name: phrases
params.label: Comma-separated search phrases (ParlInfo matches SHORT phrases; long ones return nothing)
params.default: NDIS Commission, banning order, unregistered provider, NDIS fraud

params.name: via
params.label: Record class: estimates | committees | chamber | any

lenses.name: Where competition is nominal
lenses.description: Market concentration in the window, arithmetically: per agency and per category family, the top supplier's share of value, the supplier count, and the pairs where one supplier took everything across several contracts. Concentration is a STRUCTURE observation — specialised markets concentrate for good reasons — so this lens ranks and counts, and never characterises.

lenses.name: Where the money goes
lenses.description: One window's committed value cut three ways: by CONTRACT SIZE (arithmetic bands), by CATEGORY using the government's own UNSPSC titles (deterministic — no model guesses what a code means), and by SECTOR using an LLM to classify each description into labels you supply ("weapons, software, health, transport"), which is the only cut a model is needed for and is labelled as a judgment throughout.

params.name: sectors
params.label: Sector labels for the LLM cut (comma-separated; blank = skip the model entirely)
params.default: weapons and defence materiel, software and IT, health and medical, transport and logistics, construction and property, professional and consulting services, education and training, other

lenses.name: Who gets the grants, and how fast the money moves
lenses.description: Two arithmetic questions about grant ACCESS that the published lists cannot answer separately. CONCENTRATION: per program and per agency, how much of the money went to the top recipient, how many distinct recipients shared it, and where one recipient took everything. LAG: the days from publication to start and from start to end — which shows, measured rather than assumed, that this register publishes most awards AFTER they commence, so only the extreme tail distinguishes anything. Concentration is a STRUCTURE observation — a single national body is often the only eligible recipient. Counts and dates only; no judgments anywhere in this lens.

lenses.name: Who the register's own prose names
lenses.description: The compliance register links nothing — but its NARRATIVES do. A banning order against an individual routinely names the provider they worked through; a revocation narrative names related parties. This lens reads the latest extract's full prose with an LLM extraction, keeps only names that verifiably appear in the text (a name the model returns but the corpus does not contain is DROPPED), then self-joins the corpus: an organisation appearing in the narratives of two or more DIFFERENT subjects is a cluster the Commission's own words reveal but no register field links. Around that core: what the Commission enforces per action type (themes, in the model's words, labelled as such), the published length of every ban (arithmetic over the register's own phrasing), and each named organisation checked against the ACNC disability roll. Every mention is quoted verbatim — a mention can be as employer, as victim-context, or as bystander, and only the quote says which.

lenses.name: Your theme, their money
lenses.description: Grants matched to a theme YOU define, in your own words — "youth mental health in regional areas", "flood resilience", "domestic violence prevention". GrantConnect only offers a fixed Category dropdown, and real policy questions cut straight across it: flood resilience is funded from Infrastructure, Environment, Home Affairs and emergency-management programs with no shared label anywhere. This reads every award's published PURPOSE text against your phrase, then does pure arithmetic on what matched — including the negative space: which electorates received nothing on your theme.

params.name: theme
params.label: Your theme, in your own words

params.name: strictness
params.label: How close a match must be (0.5 loose … 0.9 strict)

topic.description: A word or phrase to match in petition demands, e.g. 'animal', 'water', 'school'.

limit.description: How many seats, most signatures first.

views.name: WherePetitionIsHot
views.description: The reverse lens — pick a petition by a word from its demand and see which constituencies signed it most. Matches the most-signed open petition containing the phrase.

petition.description: A word or phrase from the petition's demand, e.g. 'water', 'surrogacy'.

limit.description: How many seats, most signatures first.

views.name: WhatMyPlacesCareAboutInBrief
views.description: One row per seat — the three petitions with the strongest local backing (per-10,000 share of each petition's national signatures), rendered as a single plain sentence. When one cause clearly outstrips the runner-up (1.5x, computed in Cypher, never judged by the model) the sentence says so, in wording that varies by seat. One model call per seat.

views.name: PayAcrossConstituencies
views.description: Median full-time annual pay for every Westminster constituency (ASHE, July 2024 boundaries), richest first — the national per-seat economic cross-section in one NOMIS call. Great Britain only: the 18 Northern Ireland seats are absent from ASHE. Pay is measured where the JOB is, not where the worker lives, so commuter seats read high.

limit.description: How many seats to return, highest pay first (the whole cross-section by default).

views.name: PayVsPetitionSigning
views.description: Does a seat's PAY predict how hard it signs a petition? For every live petition, the correlation across all 631 constituencies between what the seat earns (NOMIS ASHE) and how many people there signed (the petitions site's per-seat map) — with a confidence interval and whether the association is DETECTABLE at all, so a flat result reads as flat rather than as a small effect. A negative r means poorer seats signed harder. Joins two registers on the shared July 2024 GSS code; neither publisher holds the other's half. Association across seats, never causation, and signatures are a self-selecting sample of petition-site users, which skews by age and internet access as well as by money.

limit.description: How many live petitions to analyse (the feed's top page by default).

views.name: WhatPoorSeatsAskFor
views.description: For each of the most-signed live petitions, the average pay of the 20 constituencies that signed it HARDEST against the 20 that signed it least — the class gradient of what Britain asks Parliament for, in pounds rather than a coefficient. Joins the petitions site's per-seat signature map to NOMIS ASHE pay on the shared July 2024 GSS code. For whether a gap is statistically detectable at all, use PayVsPetitionSigning; a 20-seat contrast always produces two numbers, even when the relation is noise.

petitions.description: How many of the most-signed live petitions to analyse.

views.name: WhatPredictsSeatSigning
views.description: A least-squares fit, across all 631 constituencies, of how hard each seat signed the single most-signed live petition on what that seat EARNS — standardized beta, honest R², and the seats furthest above and below their prediction by name. The residuals are the interesting half: a seat signing far harder than its pay predicts is telling you something pay cannot explain. Joins petition signatures to NOMIS ASHE pay on the shared GSS code. Association across seats, never causation; signatures are a self-selecting sample.

views.name: DistrictCrimeLeague
views.description: England & Wales districts ranked by official recorded crime per 1,000 residents (year ending March 2024), worst first — headline rate with violence, theft and shoplifting beside it. Westminster tops any such list partly because crimes are counted where they happen and residents where they live; say so when presenting. City of London is null (supplier data unavailable). For safest-first, order ascending on the raw type.

views.name: DistrictCrimeAtMyPlaces
views.description: The official recorded-crime rates for each watched place's local authority (per 1,000 residents, year ending March 2024) — the district-wide complement to the 1-mile street view. A place in a merged authority (Buckinghamshire, East Suffolk) shows one row per legacy sub-area; a place whose district publishes only combined figures (parts of Devon, Kent, Worcestershire) shows none.

views.name: CrimeVsIncomeAcrossDistricts
views.description: Every district's official crime rate beside its median full-time pay — the national cross-section (roughly 290 districts), poorest first, so the association is visible as you read down. Crime is per 1,000 residents (year ending March 2024); pay is ASHE median gross annual pay. Association across areas, not causation, and not a claim about anyone.

limit.description: Maximum district rows (the whole cross-section by default).

views.name: WhatTracksDistrictCrime
views.description: What are the best PREDICTORS of crime — 'what drives crime', 'run a regression on crime', 'which factors explain crime levels'? One statistical answer over the whole England & Wales district cross-section: the pay–crime correlation, and a least-squares fit of the crime rate on median pay and population, standardized betas ranking the predictors, with the districts most above and below their prediction by name. Asked per constituency or per area, the DISTRICT is the statistical unit the sources share. Deterministic arithmetic over official figures — association across areas, never causation, and Westminster's daytime-population inflation applies.

views.name: WhatBestPredictsCrime
views.description: What is the best PREDICTOR of recorded crime across England — deprivation, urbanity, income, age structure, ethnic diversity, or population? A least-squares fit of each district's crime rate — offences per 1,000 RESIDENTS, the publisher's own per-capita figure, so this is not a population-size artefact — on median pay, population density, the share of residents aged 20-24, IoD2019 deprivation, ethnic DIVERSITY (an index over the whole composition — the chance two residents drawn at random belong to different groups, never any single group's share) and population together, with STANDARDIZED betas so all six are directly comparable, honest R², and the districts furthest above and below their prediction by name. Joins six registers on the district code: ONS recorded crime, NOMIS ASHE pay, Census 2021 density, Census 2021 age structure, Census 2021 ethnic composition, MHCLG IoD2019. England only once deprivation is in the fit — Wales measures deprivation on a separate, non-comparable index. Read a beta as strength of association ACROSS AREAS: it is a statement about places, never about the people in them, and a variable that looks strong alone and weak here had its apparent effect belonging to a variable it travels with. Two warnings the numbers cannot carry: recorded crime counts where offences HAPPEN and residents where they LIVE, which inflates city-centre and retail districts (Westminster above all); and R² here is modest by design — the joinable open data holds economic and structural variables, not the policing, reporting and opportunity factors that drive much of the remainder.

views.name: CrimePredictorsOneByOne
views.description: Each candidate predictor of district crime measured ALONE — deprivation, density, the 20-24 share, ethnic diversity, pay and population each correlated with the crime rate on its own, with a confidence interval and whether the association is DETECTABLE. Read beside WhatBestPredictsCrime: a variable that looks strong here and weak there is one whose apparent effect belonged to a variable it travels with. Association across areas, never causation.

views.name: CrimeModelWithPredictors
views.description: A least-squares fit of district crime rate on WHICHEVER of the six predictors the caller enables — deprivation, population density, the 20-24 share, median pay, ethnic diversity and population — with standardized betas, R², and the districts furthest above and below prediction. Enabling exactly one gives that predictor's association measured ALONE (a solo standardized beta is its correlation), so the same view answers 'what does this variable claim by itself' and 'what survives beside the others', which is the comparison that matters. The district set is identical for every combination (263, England only, since deprivation is England-only), so a beta that moves moved because the model changed, not the sample. Predictors are returned as x1..xn in this fixed order: deprivation, density, youngAdults, pay, diversity, population. Association across areas, never causation, and never a statement about any person.

youngAdults.description: Include the share of residents aged 20-24.

diversity.description: Include the ethnic diversity index (never a single group's share).

views.name: DistrictsRanked
views.description: Every English district in the crime model, worst crime rate first, with the value of each predictor beside it — deprivation, density, the 20-24 share, median pay and ethnic diversity. The same 263 districts and the same figures the model fits, so a reader can find a place they know and see where it actually sits rather than taking the coefficients on trust. Crime is offences per 1,000 residents (ONS, year ending March 2024); Westminster's is inflated by its daytime population.

limit.description: How many districts, worst crime first (the whole set by default).

views.name: CrimeAroundMyPlaces
views.description: Recorded crime around each watched UK place, latest month, by category — as a RATE per 1,000 estimated residents within the mile (census density x 8.14 km²), raw count beside it. Rate null where density is unknown (outcodes).

views.name: SafestPlace
views.description: Watched UK places ranked by recorded crime PER 1,000 estimated residents within the mile (radius count ÷ census density x 8.14 km²), safest first — a raw count rewards emptiness, so the rate is the ranking and the count rides beside it. Places without a neighbourhood density (outcodes) rank by raw count at the end. Zero can also mean Scotland or Greater Manchester, where the source has no coverage.

limit.description: How many places to return, safest first.

views.name: TopCrimeStreets
views.description: The streets with the most recorded incidents around your watched places, latest month — raw counts BY NECESSITY (no population exists for an anonymised street locality), so compare streets within one place, never places against each other; the place views carry the rates.

limit.description: Maximum streets to return, busiest first.

views.name: ViolenceAndRobbery
views.description: Violent crime and robbery around each watched place, latest month, RANKED BY RATE per 1,000 estimated residents within the mile — the categories people mean by "is it safe", corrected for how many people are actually there. Raw counts ride beside; rate null where density is unknown (outcodes rank last).

views.name: PlaceDossier
views.description: The whole picture per watched place, one row each — crime level, median income, average house price, top ethnic group, MP, party and majority. Fires every producer; the first read is the slow one.

views.name: CrimeVsIncome
views.description: Crime RATE (per 1,000 estimated residents within the mile) against the district's median full-time pay, per watched place — the affluence-and-safety scatter, population-corrected, from sources that never meet anywhere else.

views.name: MyPlaces
views.description: The places being watched — name, postcode and coordinates. The realm's roster: every other view starts from these.

views.name: PayAtMyPlaces
views.description: District median full-time annual pay (ONS ASHE) at each watched place, highest first — 'where do people earn the most among my places'. District-level: it describes where the place is, not the person next door.

limit.description: How many places to return, highest pay first.

views.name: SeatsAndMargins
views.description: Every watched place's MP, party, majority and turnout — with the district's median pay beside it, so "what do the safe seats earn" is the same table as "who holds the marginals".

views.name: IncomeByParty
views.description: Average district median pay grouped by the party holding each watched place's seat — "what does a Labour street earn vs a Reform one", computed live from ONS pay and Parliament's own record.

views.name: NeighbourhoodMosaic
views.description: Census 2021 ethnic composition of each watched place's immediate neighbourhood — five groups, percentages, LSOA-level, so two places in the same borough can still read completely differently.

views.name: WhatHomesActuallySold
views.description: The latest registered sales at each watched place's postcode — real prices paid from the Land Registry, not estimates. Empty for outcode-level places.

views.name: PriceTrendAtMyPlaces
views.description: The official average house price in each watched place's district, this month against a year ago, with the annual change computed — the estate agent's chart, from the actual index.

views.name: WhereNotToEat
views.description: Food businesses within a mile of watched places rated 2 or worse at their last official hygiene inspection — with the district's median pay beside them, because a low rating in a wealthy postcode is a story.

views.name: FloodWatch
views.description: Live Environment Agency flood alerts near watched places, worst first — empty is the answer you want.

views.name: SchoolsNearMyPlaces
views.description: Schools within 1.5 km of each watched place, from OpenStreetMap — counts plus the named ones. Where schools are, not how they are rated.

views.name: CrimeByParty
views.description: Watched places grouped by the party holding each seat, ranked within party by crime RATE per 1,000 estimated residents — "Labour seats with the lowest crime" corrected for how many people live there. Raw count beside; rate null where density is unknown.

views.name: CrimeTrend
views.description: Each watched place's monthly crime counts over the last year, with the percent change from the first to the latest month — rising first. The first run per place is twelve paced source calls; after that the past is cached and only the newest month refreshes.

views.name: OdooMeetingBriefing
views.description:
Meeting preparation: for each upcoming calendar meeting, who you are meeting, what they
owe (exact), the open deals with win odds and how their chatter threads read, who
ultimately owns them, recent news — and a composed 4-6 sentence briefing. Answers "prep
me for my meeting with X", "brief me on my upcoming meetings", "what do I need to know
before my meetings". The customer parameter narrows to one counterparty by name.

customer.description: Only meetings whose counterparty name contains this (case-insensitive). Empty = all upcoming.

views.name: OdooDealTriage
views.description:
Classify every open opportunity — strategic / standard / at_risk — and read the sentiment
of its recent interactions from the chatter thread. Answers "which deals are in trouble",
"which deals are at risk", "how do our opportunities feel", "triage the pipeline",
"understand our recent interactions", "which opportunities need attention". Sentiment is
null for a deal nobody has written on: silence is not neutral, it is unknown.

triage.description: Only deals judged this way: strategic, standard or at_risk. Empty = every open deal.

views.name: OdooPipelineReceivables
views.description: Every open opportunity at a CRM stage, with the customer it belongs to and every posted, unpaid invoice that customer still owes. One row per (opportunity, invoice); an opportunity whose customer owes nothing appears once with null invoice columns. The question this answers: "who are we trying to sell MORE to while they still owe us money?"

stage.description: The CRM stage name exactly as Odoo shows it: New, Qualified, Proposition, Won.

views.name: OdooReceivablesByCustomer
views.description: Which customers owe us money, most first: one row per customer with the count of posted unpaid invoices and the exact total still owed. THE answer for "who owes us most", "who still hasn't paid us", "unpaid customers", "our most valuable customer by outstanding balance", "total receivables per customer". The payment-status filter is INSIDE the view (posted invoices, not fully paid) — it needs no parameter to express it. Grouping is by customer id, so duplicate names and duplicate invoice names cannot inflate or merge anything.

views.name: OdooOpenPipeline
views.description: The open pipeline: every open opportunity with its customer, stage and expected revenue, highest value first. THE answer for "what deals are open", "pipeline by customer", "biggest open opportunities" — including probability-filtered forms ("over 60%", "likely to close") via minProbability.

minProbability.description: Only opportunities at or above this win probability percent (e.g. 60).

views.name: OdooWins
views.description: Deals WON, biggest first: each won opportunity with its customer, value and close date. THE answer for "our biggest win", "what did we win last quarter/month", "recent wins", "deals closed won". Pass since/until as ISO dates (e.g. '2026-04-01') to window by close date; omit them for all time.

since.description: Earliest close date, ISO (inclusive). Empty = no lower bound.

until.description: Latest close date, ISO (inclusive day; compares as string). Empty = no upper bound.

views.name: OdooCustomerCount
views.description: How many customers are on the book — one row, one number. THE answer for "how many customers do we have", "number of clients/accounts".

views.name: OdooOutstandingInvoices
views.description: The outstanding invoices themselves, biggest first: each posted unpaid customer invoice with its customer, amount still owed and due date. THE answer for "biggest outstanding invoices", "largest unpaid invoices", "top overdue invoices", "which invoices are open".

views.name: OdooCompanies
views.description: Every company the CRM knows — customers and prospects — with its website. THE answer for "which companies are in the CRM". Reading it also keys each of them to the business vocabulary's CustomerAccount, which is how an account-level surface comes to know about a company sales is courting and nobody bills yet.

views.name: HealthAtRiskAccounts
views.description: The accounts that are AT RISK, and every reason why: owing money while waiting on support, an open deal while a case is open, a failed payment, a renewal coming with a case open, a very long open thread, high-priority cases, or being billed with no owner in the CRM. THE answer for "which accounts are at risk", "which customers are in trouble", "why is <customer> at risk" and "who needs attention". A reason that does not apply is null.

account.description: Only this account, by company domain (e.g. wayne-ent.com). Empty = every account at risk.

views.name: HealthSharedIssues
views.description: Pairs of accounts that each have an open support case in the SAME product area, with the areas they share. THE answer for "is this one unhappy customer or an incident", "which customers have the same problem" and "what else is affected by <area>".

views.name: HealthPossiblyWithheld
views.description: Unpaid invoices on accounts that raised a still-open support case BEFORE the invoice fell due — money collections should not chase without knowing about the problem. THE answer for "are any customers withholding payment over a problem" and "which unpaid invoices are tied to a support case". It shows the two facts and their order; it does not claim the customer said so.

views.name: HealthOpenCaseCountsByAccount
views.description: Per account: HOW MANY support cases a customer is still waiting on — the count, how many are high priority or urgent, the longest back-and-forth, and when the oldest was opened. THE answer for "which customers have open support cases" and "who is waiting on us" across the whole book. An account absent from this list has nothing open. For WHAT the cases are about, ask HealthOpenCasesByAccount about the accounts this names.

views.name: HealthUrgentCaseCountsByAccount
views.description: Per account: how many of the open support cases are URGENT or HIGH priority. The escalation signal behind HealthOpenCaseCountsByAccount — an account absent from this list has open cases but none of them urgent.

views.name: HealthOpenCasesByAccount
views.description: Per account: WHAT the open support cases are about — their subjects and ids, alongside the same counts. The detail behind HealthOpenCaseCountsByAccount, for a named account or a short list of them. Reads every open case it reports on, so ask it about the accounts you care about rather than the whole book.

views.name: HealthResolvedCasesByAccount
views.description: Per account: the support cases that have been RESOLVED — how many, when the latest was closed, and what they were about. THE answer for "what have we fixed for <customer>" and "who have we recently helped".

views.name: HealthReceivablesByAccount
views.description: Per account, MOST OWED FIRST: what is owed and not collected — the amount, unpaid invoices counted, how many FAILED collection, and links to the invoices. THE answer for "which accounts owe us the most", "which accounts owe us money", "who owes us the most money" and "who has a failed payment". "The most" means the largest AMOUNT, never the most invoices. An account absent from this list owes nothing.

views.name: HealthBillingByAccount
views.description: Per account: every invoice billing has issued them, and how many were paid. THE answer for "is <customer> a good payer" and the way to tell a billed account from one billing has never heard of. An account absent from this list is not billed.

views.name: HealthRecurringByAccount
views.description: Per account: what they pay on a schedule — active subscriptions, the amount per billing period, what the products are, and when the next one renews. THE answer for "how much is <customer> worth to us", "who are our biggest customers" and "who renews soon". Amounts are per billing period as the plan defines it; do not annualize them.

views.name: HealthPipelineByAccount
views.description: Per account: the deals sales has with them — open pipeline value, the open deals by name, when the next is due to close, and how many were won and lost. THE answer for "what are we trying to sell <customer>" and "how much pipeline do we have with <customer>". An account absent from this list has no deal in the CRM, open or closed.

views.name: HealthCrmRecordByAccount
views.description: Per account: the CRM's own record of it. THE way to tell an account sales knows from one it does not: an account absent from this list has no record in the CRM at all, however much it is billed or however many cases it has open.

views.name: HealthCompanyNotesForOpenCases
views.description: For every account with an open support case: the notes on the company's own CRM record, with their text and date. Part of "does the CRM know about this customer's problem".

views.name: HealthDealNotesForOpenCases
views.description: For every account with an open support case: the notes on its DEALS in the CRM, with their text, date and the deal they are on.

views.name: HealthContactNotesForOpenCases
views.description: For every account with an open support case: the notes on the PEOPLE the CRM knows there, with their text, date and who they are about.

views.name: HealthSellingIntoTrouble
views.description: Accounts where sales has an OPEN DEAL and the customer has an OPEN SUPPORT CASE, largest deal first — with the longest thread and what it is about. THE answer for "are we about to pitch an unhappy customer", "which deals are at risk from support problems" and "what should sales know before the next call".

views.name: HealthOwingAndWaiting
views.description: Accounts with OPEN SUPPORT CASES AND UNPAID INVOICES at the same time, most owed first. THE answer for "which accounts have open support cases and unpaid invoices", "who owes us money and is waiting on support" and "who is not paying and also has a problem open" — the accounts where a collections call and a support fix are the same conversation.

views.name: HealthRevenueBehindCases
views.description: Recurring revenue sitting behind open support cases: every paying account with something open, what it pays per billing period, and when it next renews. THE answer for "how much revenue is at risk from open support cases" and "which unhappy customers renew soonest".

views.name: HealthBilledButUnknownToCrm
views.description: Customers we BILL that the CRM has NO RECORD of. THE answer for "who are we billing that the CRM has no record of", "who are we billing that sales has never heard of", "which paying customers are missing from the CRM" and "which customers have no account owner". These are business customers in the billing system — nothing to do with the user's own household bills.

views.name: HealthCaseTriage
views.description: Every open support case, judged from the customer's own words: IMPACT on their business (blocked, degraded, inconvenienced, or merely asking for something) and their MOOD toward us (frustrated, neutral, positive). THE answer for "which customers are really hurting", "which support cases are serious", "who is frustrated with us" and "which open cases matter" — a 42-reply thread about dark mode is not trouble, and a 7-reply thread from a blocked customer is. Cases with no message from the customer are absent: there is nothing to judge.

views.name: HealthCrmAwareness
views.description: For every account with an open support case that the CRM tracks: does ANYTHING sales has written — on the company, its deals or its people — touch the topic of what support is dealing with? `aware` or `unaware`, judged by a model from the notes and the case subjects. THE answer for "does sales know about this customer's problem", "which open cases are not reflected in the CRM" and "where is sales blind". One opinion: check it against the notes.

views.name: ChatwootOpenCases
views.description: Every case a customer is still waiting on: open conversations, most urgent first and the longest-running thread first within a priority. THE answer for "what support cases are open", "what are customers waiting on", "open high priority tickets" (via priority) and "what is open for <company>" (via account, the company's domain).

priority.description: Only this priority: urgent, high, medium or low. Empty = every priority.

account.description: Only this customer, by company domain (e.g. wayne-ent.com). Empty = every customer.

views.name: ChatwootOpenCasesByAccount
views.description: Open cases counted per customer, busiest first, with how many of them are high priority or worse. THE answer for "which customers have the most open support cases" and "who is struggling". A customer absent from this list has nothing open — that is an answer.

views.name: ChatwootCaseCounts
views.description: How many cases the desk holds in each status. THE answer for "how many support cases are open" and "how many have we resolved".

views.name: ChatwootCompanies
views.description: Every company that has ever raised a case, with how many and how many are still open. THE answer for "which companies does support deal with". Reading it also keys each of them to the business vocabulary's CustomerAccount, which is how an account-level surface comes to know about a company only support has heard of.

views.name: LagoUnpaidInvoices
views.description: Every bill that has been issued and not yet collected, largest first: payment pending, or tried and FAILED. THE answer for "who owes us money", "unpaid invoices", "failed payments" (via paymentStatus = failed) and "what does <customer> owe" (via customer, a name fragment). NOT an answer to anything about RETRIES or ATTEMPTS — how many times a payment was tried is not recorded here, and "failed" is not "retried". NOT an answer to a question that also mentions support cases, deals or the CRM: billing alone cannot see those.

paymentStatus.description: Only this payment status: pending or failed. Empty = both.

customer.description: Only customers whose name contains this. Empty = every customer.

views.name: LagoReceivablesByCustomer
views.description: What each customer owes, most first: unpaid invoices counted and summed per customer, with how many of them have FAILED collection. THE answer for "which customers owe the most" and "who has failed payments". A customer absent from this list owes nothing — that is an answer. Billing ONLY: a question that also mentions support cases, deals or the CRM is an account-level question and this view would silently drop that half of it.

views.name: LagoRecurringRevenue
views.description: What each customer pays on a schedule: their ACTIVE subscriptions counted and summed per billing period, largest first. THE answer for "who are our biggest customers", "how much recurring revenue is at stake with <customer>" and "what is <customer> subscribed to". Amounts are per billing period as the plan defines it — Lago's listing does not say whether that is a month or a year, so do not annualize these figures. Billing ONLY: for revenue "behind open support cases", "at risk" or tied to deals, this view would silently drop the condition — that is an account-level question.

views.name: LagoPaymentStatusCounts
views.description: How many issued invoices are in each payment status, and what they total. THE answer for "how is collection going" and the figure to reconcile this realm against Lago with.

views.name: LagoCustomers
views.description: Everybody billing invoices: name, website, billing email, currency and since when. THE answer for "who are our billing customers". Reading it also keys every one of them to the business vocabulary's CustomerAccount, which is how an account-level surface comes to know about a customer only billing has heard of.

views.name: RobotQueueNow
views.description: The Lumina Robot queue RIGHT NOW: pending items per queue type and sub-type and how long the oldest has waited. Read live from the monitoring stored procedure on every call — never cached, so the answer is as of this second, not as of the last Datadog poll.

views.name: DbConnectionsNow
views.description: Database connections RIGHT NOW by login, host, database and program, with whether any session in the group is blocked. Read live from the monitoring stored procedure on every call.

views.name: InvoiceErrorsByCompany
views.description: Which client companies have failed invoices, on which integration, and how many — the Expense IQ 'who is affected' question. Joins the audit trail to company and connector so the answer names companies, never GUIDs.

views.name: RecentPipelineRuns
views.description: The most recent CloverDX pipeline runs per connector with their outcome and error message — did last night's runs succeed, and if not, why.

views.name: InvoiceErrorsForBrand
views.description: Invoice processing errors for one FCTG brand over the last 30 days, per company and connector, with a sample error message — from a parameterised stored procedure that takes the brand as its argument.

brand.description: The brand: Corporate Traveller or FCM Travel.

views.name: ActionsRunCount
views.description: SELECT THIS for any COUNT or RATE over a repository's runs: "how many workflow runs did owner/repo have in the last N days", "how many builds failed in owner/repo in the last N days", "what is the CI success rate for owner/repo", "how many builds ran". One row: runs, completed, succeeded, failed, cancelled, successRatePct. Do not compose these from the runs; this view is the figure.

days.description: Window in days ending now, at most 31 (the history door's depth); ignored when since is given.

since.description: ISO-8601 lower bound on created_at, e.g. 2026-09-16T00:00:00Z; overrides days. The history door holds 31 days, so an earlier bound is silently the 31-day floor.

views.name: ActionsRunTime
views.description: SELECT THIS for "what is the average build time", "how long do builds take", "mean run time", "average duration of CI", "typical build time" — for one repository (repo) or across every followed repository (repo empty). One row over the window: completed runs, average, median-ish (the run at the 50th position), 90th-percentile and longest run time in minutes, average queue seconds. Run time is updated_at − run_started_at on a completed run.

repo.description: Repository as owner/repo; empty = every followed repository.

days.description: Window in days ending now, at most 31; ignored when since is given.

since.description: ISO-8601 lower bound on created_at; overrides days.

views.name: ActionsByActor
views.description: Who triggers the runs: per actor over a window, runs triggered, how many failed, and the failure rate — most runs first. "Who triggered the most runs", "who runs the most builds", "runs by person", "who breaks the build most". NOTE: this realm holds no commits; actor is the GitHub login whose push, pull request or dispatch started the run.

repo.description: Repository as owner/repo; empty = every followed repository.

days.description: Window in days ending now, at most 31; ignored when since is given.

since.description: ISO-8601 lower bound on created_at; overrides days.

views.name: ActionsRecentRuns
views.description: The runs in a window, newest first, each with its workflow, branch, trigger, conclusion, queue time and run time in seconds, who triggered it, and its link. The base list — "show me this week's builds", "recent runs on main", "what ran today".

views.name: NdisDisabilityFilers
views.description: FY2024 Annual Information Statements of charities that declared a disability program — the candidate set every screen starts from. Composable: traverse from it to the charity register, the compliance register or the ABN register.

classification.description: ACNC program classification (Disability services, Disability sports, Housing for people with disabilities, Disabled persons' rights, Family disability resources).

views.name: NdisWorkforceFlip
views.description: Providers whose employee expenses collapsed as a share of service revenue between FY23 and FY24 while revenue held or grew — the work is now done by someone other than employees. Lawful, and the documented precondition of both sham contracting and billing intermediation.

minService.description: Floor on FY24 service revenue (government + goods and services).

views.name: NdisMoneyLeavesUnspecified
views.description: Providers where most money leaves as unspecified "all other expenses" rather than wages or named grants — the brokerage / plan-management shape. Lawful and common, and the one place where public money's ultimate recipient is named in no public register.

minOtherShare.description: Minimum percentage of total expenses booked as 'all other expenses'.

views.name: NdisRevenueSurgeWithoutStaff
views.description: Providers whose service revenue multiplied year on year while full-time-equivalent staff did not — the shape a phantom-services claim would have to survive. A capital grant, a merger or a first full year of operation produces it innocently.

minMultiple.description: Minimum year-on-year revenue multiple, in hundredths (250 = 2.5x).

views.name: NdisSelfContradictingFiling
views.description: Filings that disagree with themselves — government revenue above total revenue, or employee expenses reported with zero full-time-equivalent staff. Most often a keying error, which is itself worth knowing about a self-reported dataset used to hold providers to account.

views.name: NdisEnforcementWaves
views.description: Compliance notices grouped by the day they took effect. The register is not a stream of individual findings: notices arrive in mass batches on single dates, so a provider's presence in it may mean only that it sat inside one.

snapshotKey.description: Which dated extract to read: 'datasetId|resourceId|filename' from the data.gov.au catalogue.

minNotices.description: Only report days with at least this many notices.

views.name: NdisRegisterOpacity
views.description: How specifically the register explains itself, per action type: how many rows state a basis ("on the basis that…", "reasonably believes", "convicted of") versus only describing what is prohibited or required. Banning orders publish scope, not conduct — this counts it.

views.name: NdisNewEnforcement
views.description: Actions present in one dated extract and absent from an earlier one — enforcement that APPEARED, which no single extract shows. An appearance is dated to the interval between two extracts, not to a day: the register's own effective date frequently precedes publication by months, and a row appearing now may concern conduct years old.

newerSnapshot.description: The later extract: 'datasetId|resourceId|filename' from the data.gov.au catalogue.

olderSnapshot.description: The earlier extract to diff against.

views.name: NdisNewEnforcementRead
views.description: The same arrivals, restricted to banning orders and revocations, with the Commission's narrative READ: a one-label reading of what the text attributes the action to, and whether it states any reason at all. The label is a MODEL's reading of the register's words; the verbatim narrative is on every row beside it. Banning-order narratives mostly state the scope of the prohibition and not the conduct, so 'not stated' is the expected answer, and it is the finding.

olderSnapshot.description: The earlier extract to diff against.

views.name: NdisProviderPurposes
views.description: Semantic groups over the only narrative field in the Annual Information Statement — how each charity says it pursued its purposes. Sizes are counted, not estimated, so "how many of these providers describe accommodation" is arithmetic over the rows the traversal returned. Self- reported prose: it describes what a provider CLAIMS to do, which is exactly its value beside the money columns.

classification.description: ACNC program classification whose filers to read.

groups.description: How many semantic groups to form.

views.name: NdisProviderPurposesForTheFlagged
views.description: The same free text, restricted to the providers whose money leaves as unspecified "other expenses" — reading what the pass-through cohort says it does. A brokerage or plan-management description explains the shape innocently; a direct-service description alongside near-zero labour cost does not, and is worth a human's attention.

views.name: NdisProgramMix
views.description: Semantic groups over the program NAMES a cohort declared — the register's own taxonomy is only five disability classes wide, but providers name their programs freely, and the names say more about what is delivered than the class does.

classification.description: ACNC program classification whose program names to group.

groups.description: How many semantic groups to form.

views.name: NdisPersonPressTrail
views.description: News-index results for one person named in an NDIS compliance action. The search phrase is built per invocation as the person's exact quoted name plus NDIS, making this a separate virtual Cypher traversal for each card rather than part of the register-diff finding. A result is third-party material whose index text matched that phrase: names collide, snippets are not verified facts, and no result may be used to create, suppress or strengthen a register finding. Every row retains the searched phrase, headline, snippet, freshness and URL so the citizen can open the publisher's page and judge it.

person.description: Person's name exactly as published in the compliance register.

views.name: NdisProviderLegalTrail
views.description: Tribunal and court documents naming a provider, read. The search is an EXACT QUOTED PHRASE scoped to austlii.edu.au, so a hit is a document containing that provider's name — but a name can appear as a party, a witness, an employer, a cited authority, or belong to a same-named entity, and the document itself is the evidence. The reading says whether the text looks like an employment or underpayment matter (the independent test for a workforce-model flip) and whether the provider appears to be a party.

provider.description: Provider name to search, exactly as it should appear in documents.

views.name: NdisFlaggedProviderLegalTrail
views.description: Every provider whose workforce model flipped, paired with the tribunal and court record. A flip is lawful and ordinary; a flip ALONGSIDE an employment or underpayment matter is corroborated by an independent source. OPTIONAL MATCH is deliberate: a provider with no documents must still appear, with zero, because "searched and found nothing" and "never searched" are different facts and an inner join cannot tell them apart.

views.name: ContractsBySize
views.description: A window's contracts in FIXED value bands, with each band's share. The bands are fixed so two windows are comparable, and they show directly what a total conceals: Commonwealth contracting is extremely top-heavy, with a handful of notices carrying most of the value.

views.name: ContractsByMethod
views.description: Procurement method by BOTH measures — share of notice count and share of value. Reporting one without the other misleads: a method can dominate the number of notices while carrying little value, or the reverse, and the register supports neither claim alone.

views.name: LimitedTenderGrounds
views.description: The stated grounds for limited tenders, ranked by value and count, in the register's own wording. A ground is the AGENCY'S STATED REASON — never an assessment of that reason, and never evidence that a limited tender was improper.

views.name: SupplierConcentration
views.description: How concentrated a window is: each agency's total, its supplier count, and the share taken by its largest supplier. This is what a headline total conceals — a big number is often the story of one or two notices. Supplier names are grouped case-insensitively with separators stripped; that is a NAME grouping, not entity resolution, and a group may span or split real entities.

minAgencyValue.description: Only report agencies committing at least this much in the window.

views.name: NewSuppliersInWindow
views.description: Suppliers holding a contract in this window that held none in an earlier one — first APPEARANCES in the published register, which is not the same as new businesses: a supplier absent from the earlier window may have been contracting for decades, or may appear under a differently-spelled name. Uses the collect-and-exclude shape rather than a subquery, since the scope rewriter rejects subqueries.

priorWindow.description: The earlier window to compare against.

minValue.description: Only report suppliers whose new-window commitments reach this.

views.name: SupplierTaxTransparency
views.description: A window's largest suppliers joined by ABN to the ATO corporate tax transparency report. TWO published caveats travel with every row: a BLANK taxable income or tax payable means '<= 0' BY LEGISLATION (amounts of zero or less may not be reported), never 'unknown'; and the report is ENTITY-level, not consolidated groups, so the contracting entity is frequently not the reporting entity. Absence from the report usually means income under the $100m threshold.

minValue.description: Only screen suppliers committing at least this much in the window.

views.name: ThinDisclosureLargeCommitments
views.description: Large commitments whose published description does not let a reader identify what was bought. Brevity alone is NOT the finding: a short description naming a specific place, period or item discloses perfectly well, and only the model's reading decides. This measures what was PUBLISHED, never what was procured — lawful confidentiality exists, national security among other grounds, so a low score is a reason to go and read the record and never evidence of wrongdoing. Descriptions are returned verbatim so a reader sees the vacuum rather than a paraphrase of it.

minAmount.description: Only commitments at or above this value (AUD).

maxChars.description: The GATE, not a verdict: only descriptions this short are read by the model. Raising it reads more rows and costs more; it never makes a row a finding on its own.

maxDisclosure.description: Report rows the model scores below this (0..1). Higher reports more.
